sections.html:
Cambridge is a Middlesex County city facing Boston across the Charles River. The 2020 census counted 118,403 residents, and its ZIP codes run from 02138 to 02142. Land area is 6.4 square miles, so houses, triple-deckers and condos sit close together.

The city calls itself a city of squares. Most commercial districts form at big street intersections that double as neighborhood centers, which is how locals say where a house is.

sections.h2: Squares and neighborhoods buyers ask about
sections.html:
Buyers usually want to know which square a house is nearest.

  • Kendall Square, at Broadway, Main Street and Third Street, is the biotech and technology center beside MIT and the Kendall/MIT Red Line station.
  • Central Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Prospect Street and Western Avenue, has a Red Line stop.
  • Harvard Square, at Massachusetts Avenue, Brattle Street and JFK Street, has the Harvard Red Line station and Cambridge Common nearby.
  • Porter Square has a Red Line stop and a Fitchburg Line commuter rail stop.
  • Inman Square sits at Cambridge and Hampshire Streets, and Lechmere Square is next to CambridgeSide.

Cambridgeport, Baldwin and Mid-Cambridge fill out the map, and each has its own mix of houses. Naming the nearest square in your listing gives a buyer an instant picture of the location.

The MBTA Red Line is the spine of the city, with stops at Kendall/MIT, Central, Harvard and Porter. Harvard Square is also a major bus terminal. If your house is a short walk from a Red Line stop, put it in the description, because it often matters more to a buyer than square footage.

The Assessing Department values property at full and fair cash value, which Massachusetts defines as 100 percent of fair market value. Appraisers weigh cost, income and market approaches, and the state Department of Revenue certifies the values before bills go out.

The city says owner-occupants can lower their bill through the residential exemption, and the FY27 application is due April 1, 2027. The Assessing page carries the current schedule, including the yearly abatement window.

sections.h2: Municipal lien certificates and water liens
sections.html:
A municipal lien certificate shows what is owed on a property, and a closing attorney will want one. Order it through the Finance Department at 617-349-4220.

Cambridge runs its own water system. A first-half FY27 tax bill can carry a Water and Sewer Lien, so read your bill closely. If one appears, phone the Finance Department before you list or sign a contract, so the balance does not surface at the closing table.

Cambridge houses often come with complications: older construction, multi-unit buildings, tenants and historic districts.

  • Tenants in a two- or three-family can affect showings and the closing date.
  • Estate sales take time because of probate.
  • Condominium sales require documents from the association.
  • Older houses may need work before a buyer's lender will move forward.

None of these are city rules. They are common snags, and most of them add weeks. If one describes your situation, a direct cash sale avoids the showings and repairs.

sections.h2: What do you need to sell a house in Cambridge?
sections.html:
The deed excise tax is $2.00 for each $500 of price or fraction of $500 under MGL c. 64D, s. 1, and the registry of deeds takes it when the deed is recorded. The local fire department must also certify that your smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale rules, a requirement from the Department of Fire Services.

The department charges a fee, so book the visit once you have a closing date. Alarms that are ten years old or past expiration have to be swapped for ten-year sealed photoelectric models with a hush feature.

Collect the deed, your newest tax bill, any lien information and permit records before you meet a buyer or attorney.

A sale here follows a familiar order. You accept an offer, sign a purchase agreement, clear any lien certificate items, pass the fire department inspection, and then sign the deed at closing. Condo owners add one more task: request the association's documents early, since waiting on them is a common cause of delay.

Cash Home Buyers can review a Cambridge house as it stands and give you a written number to compare with a listing. Without showings, a lender's appraisal or repair negotiations, you set the pace, and the closing date can follow your schedule, whether that means a lab contract starting soon or an estate that needs to wrap up.

sections.h2: Preparing the house and the paperwork
sections.html:
Start with the paper. A tidy folder saves days later. Pull the deed, the latest tax bill, any lien information and permit records for work you have done, especially kitchens, baths, additions and any finished attic or basement space. Buyers and their attorneys ask about permits on older Cambridge buildings, and a missing record can stall a closing.

For the house itself, an honest look at the roof, heating system, windows and wiring tells you whether a buyer's inspector will find surprises. Cosmetic work matters less than the big systems. If you cannot afford or do not want to do repairs, selling as is shifts that question to the buyer's price.

sections.h2: Selling an inherited or tenant-occupied house
sections.html:
Probate controls the timeline on an estate sale, and the personal representative usually cannot sign a deed until the court gives the go-ahead. Talk to an attorney about what is required first, then gather the death certificate paperwork, the deed and the tax bills.

With tenants, read each lease for its end date and notice terms. Showings need advance notice, and a buyer who plans to live in the unit may want it empty at closing. A cash buyer can often work around occupied units, which is why many Cambridge landlords and heirs ask about it.

Condominium sellers should ask the association for the master deed, the budget, the rules and any statement of unpaid fees well before listing. Multi-unit owners should tally rents, leases and any shared-system repairs. Organized files, handed over early and in one place, make a buyer more comfortable and shorten the time between agreement and closing, which matters whether the buyer is paying cash or relying on a lender.

Some owners simply want a clean exit: a landlord tired of vacancies, heirs sharing an inherited two-family, or a household moving for a new job. In each case the question is whether time or a listing's potential extra price matters more. Ask each side to put terms in writing. Compare a written cash offer against an agent's estimate, subtract the repair costs and carrying costs, and choose the one that fits your calendar.

faqs.q: What county is Cambridge, MA in?
faqs.a: Middlesex County. The city faces Boston across the Charles River.
The 2020 census counted 118,403 people, fourth in the state behind Boston, Worcester and Springfield.

faqs.q: When is the residential exemption deadline in Cambridge?
faqs.a: Applications for fiscal year 2027, residential or personal, are due April 1, 2027.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Cambridge Assessing Department?
faqs.a: Call 617-349-4343 or stop by 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor. Lien certificates go through the Finance Department at 617-349-4220.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke detector certificate to sell in Cambridge?
faqs.a: Yes. A compliance certificate from the local fire department is required by the state whenever a home is sold or transferred.
